headline: Strait of Hormuz Reopens as Oil Collapses 34% from Peak; Canada Adds 14,000 Jobs, Unemployment Holds 6.7%
executive_summary:
The Strait of Hormuz reopened on April 17 following a temporary ceasefire agreed April 8, ending what the International Energy Agency characterized as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, affecting 20% of global supplies.38 WTI crude collapsed from a peak near US$128/bbl on April 2 to US$83.85/bbl on April 17, a decline of approximately 34% in 15 trading days.40 Brent crude settled at US$90.38/bbl, down 9.0% in the April 17 session alone.15 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) and 367 mining projects ($159.5B) with direct commodity price exposure.14

Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March, a partial recovery after February's 84,000-job loss.2 National unemployment held at 6.7%, with the participation rate unchanged at 64.9% and the employment rate at 60.6%.2 Average hourly wages accelerated to +4.7% year-over-year ($37.73/hr), the fastest pace since October 2024, with workers aged 55 and older recording +5.2% and those aged 15-24 at +1.8%.2 Health care posted the largest year-over-year gain at +94,000 (+3.3%), while natural resources added 10,000 (+3.0%) in the month.2 The pipeline tracks 259 healthcare projects and 427 combined mining and oil and gas projects ($259.7B) in the affected sectors.

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February from a revised $4.2B in January, the largest since August 2025.6 Exports rose 6.4% to $66.3B — the highest since March 2025 — while imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.6 Manufacturing sales rebounded 3.6% to $71.2B in February, led by transportation equipment (+18.8%) and primary metals (+4.9% to a record $6.5B), with unfilled manufacturing orders reaching a record $117.6B.8 Housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus, while the MLS Home Price Index declined for a 16th consecutive month (-0.4% month-over-month).5

The Bloomberg-Nanos Consumer Confidence Index fell to 46.93, an 11-month low, with the expectations sub-index losing nearly 10 points over four weeks.30 The Bank of Canada rate decision on April 29 — accompanied by the Monetary Policy Report — and the federal Spring Economic Update on April 28 are the principal scheduled events in the coming week, with the March CPI release on April 20 expected to capture initial effects of the oil price surge.1343

national.analysis:
Real GDP contracted 0.2% quarter-over-quarter (-0.6% annualized) in Q4 2025, down from +0.6% in Q3, according to Statistics Canada.4 The monthly GDP print recorded a -0.6% month-over-month contraction in the latest release.54 Manufacturing GDP (NAICS 31-33) fell 1.4% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year, while management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) recorded the deepest annual contraction among 20 industries at -21.9% year-over-year.54 Construction GDP (NAICS 23) rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, while mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21) gained 1.2% month-over-month against a -0.1% annual base.54 Wholesale trade (NAICS 41) declined 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year; transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) fell 0.7% month-over-month against a +1.6% annual base.54

The Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March after February's -84,000 loss, leaving unemployment unchanged at 6.7%.2 The provincial range ran from Saskatchewan at 5.0% to Newfoundland and Labrador at 9.5%.2 By industry, other services added +15,000 (+1.9%), professional services +12,000, and natural resources +10,000 (+3.0%), while finance, insurance, and real estate shed 11,000 and accommodation and food services lost 10,000 (-0.9%).2 Average hourly wages rose 4.7% year-over-year to $37.73/hr; composition-adjusted wage growth ran at +3.6%.2 Construction employment stood at 1,998,800, manufacturing at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction at 350,300.55

Headline CPI registered +1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, within the Bank of Canada's 1-3% target band, with provincial dispersion spanning 6.5 percentage points from PE at +5.4% to ON at -1.1%.3 Core CPI median ran at 2.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, food CPI at +5.3%, and energy CPI at -14.2%.56 The March CPI release, scheduled for April 20, is expected to capture initial effects of the oil price surge from the Strait of Hormuz disruption.3

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February from a revised $4.2B in January, the largest since August 2025.6 Exports rose 6.4% to $66.3B while imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.6 Manufacturing sales rebounded 3.6% to $71.2B, led by transportation equipment (+18.8%) and primary metals (+4.9% to a record $6.5B).8 Unfilled manufacturing orders reached a record $117.6B.8 Building permits dropped 8.4% to $12.1B in February, with non-residential leading the decline at -$1.3B while residential added $135.6M.7

CMHC housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus.5 The six-month trend decreased 2.9% to 248,378.5 Year-to-date actual starts ran +9% year-over-year at 49,206 units through March.5 CREA downgraded its home sales forecast citing the oil shock but maintained a +1.5% annual price gain projection to $688,955.51 The MLS HPI declined for a 16th consecutive month at -0.4% month-over-month, and the national average home price stood at $673,084 (-0.8% year-over-year).9 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25%, the seventh consecutive hold, with the Summary of Deliberations published April 1 noting near-term growth weaker than the January projection.112 Market pricing reflects a 96.5% probability of a hold at the April 29 decision.13

consumer_pulse:
The Bloomberg-Nanos Consumer Confidence Index declined to 46.93 in the week ended April 3, an 11-month low, down from 47.50 in the prior period.30 The expectations sub-index lost nearly 10 points over four weeks, a deterioration linked to the Iran war entering its sixth week, elevated energy prices from the Strait of Hormuz disruption, and rising inflation concerns.30 Gasoline prices — driven by WTI swinging between $80.56 and $117.63 over the two-week coverage window — were the dominant cost-of-living concern in consumer sentiment tracking.14

Headline CPI at +1.8% year-over-year remains within the Bank of Canada's target band, but component dispersion is wide: food CPI ran at +5.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, and energy CPI at -14.2% — a figure that predates the oil price surge and is expected to shift materially in the March CPI release on April 20.356 Provincial CPI ranges from PE at +5.4% to ON at -1.1%, a 6.5 percentage-point spread.3 Average hourly wages at $37.73 (+4.7% year-over-year) outpaced headline CPI by 2.9 percentage points, though workers aged 15-24 recorded only +1.8% wage growth, trailing inflation in food-heavy consumption baskets.2

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7B in January, with the advance February estimate at +0.9%.53 Housing affordability remained a persistent theme: the MLS HPI fell for a 16th consecutive month, national average home price stood at $673,084 (-0.8% year-over-year), and CREA downgraded its sales forecast citing the oil shock while maintaining a +1.5% annual price gain projection to $688,955.951 National inventory reached 5 months of supply.51

global.analysis:
The US Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50-3.75%31 on March 18, maintaining a 125-150 basis point gap above the Bank of Canada overnight rate of 2.25%.1 The FOMC continues to signal one rate cut in 2026 and one in 2027.31 US unemployment stood at 4.4% in the February print.31 CAD/USD strengthened to 0.7305 on April 17, up 1.5% over the two-week period, driven in part by broader US dollar depreciation as the DXY index moved toward 98.05.27

US equity benchmarks posted record closes in the second week of the coverage window. The S&P 500 reached 7,022.95 on April 13, within 2.32% of its January 27 all-time high, after recording its best week since November.2526 The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both posted fresh record closes on April 14.25 The US Supreme Court struck down several IEEPA emergency tariffs during the period, and the administration announced a temporary 10% global tariff largely exempting CUSMA-compliant goods.42 Section 232 tariffs were restructured on April 6 with a 50% rate on core metal imports including aluminum, steel, and copper — directly affecting Canadian metal exporters.42 Canada responded on April 15 with a six-month pause on tariffs for US-origin manufacturing inputs.42

global.analysis:
China's Q1 2026 GDP grew 5.0% year-over-year, beating the 4.8% consensus and accelerating from 4.5% in Q4 2025, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.32 Industrial production rose 6.1% year-over-year, with high-tech manufacturing up 12.5% and equipment manufacturing up 8.9%.32 Exports grew 2.5% year-over-year in March (USD terms), down sharply from +21.8% in the January-February combined period, while imports surged 27.8% in March, the strongest since November 2021.33 Factory-gate prices turned positive for the first time in more than three years on soaring commodity prices.32

China's import surge supports demand for Canadian commodity exports across iron ore, copper, potash, and energy products. The pipeline tracks 367 mining projects ($159.5B) and 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) with exposure to Chinese commodity demand.32 USD/CNY stood at 6.8287 on April 8, down 1.0% month-over-month and 7.0% year-over-year, reflecting yuan appreciation against the US dollar.27 The factory-gate price reversal to positive territory indicates sustained commodity price support for Canadian resource exporters, at a time when WTI has retraced 34% from its April 2 peak on the Strait of Hormuz reopening.40

global.analysis:
The European Central Bank main refinancing rate stood at 2.15% with the deposit facility at 2.0%.34 A hold is expected at the April 29-30 meeting, with markets pricing a hike in June to 2.5% or above.35 The ECB raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 2.6% from the prior projection, citing higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict, and warned of a "layer cake of shocks" from geopolitical developments.35 Eurozone HICP ran at +1.9% year-over-year in the December 2025 print, the latest captured in the data set.34

EUR/USD traded at 1.1696 on April 9, up 1.34% on the week and +6.79% year-over-year.34 The euro's appreciation against the US dollar affects cross-border pricing of Canadian exports to the EU. If the ECB hikes to 2.5% or above in June, the narrowing rate differential with the Bank of Canada at 2.25% could influence capital flows and the EUR/CAD cross.35 The DAX closed at 24,080.63, reflecting European equity market strength during the period.34

The Bank of England base rate stood at 3.75%, 150 basis points above the Bank of Canada overnight rate of 2.25%.36 The next BoE decision is April 30; 90% of Reuters-surveyed economists expect a hold, while 5 expect a 25 basis point hike.52 UK CPI at 3.0% exceeds the 2% target and contrasts with Canada's 1.8%, reflecting divergent inflation dynamics driven in part by the UK's greater exposure to European energy markets and domestic services inflation.36 Pre-Iran-war expectations of two 2026 rate cuts have been abandoned; markets are split between a hold and a hike.52

GBP/USD traded at 1.3432, up 1.5% week-over-week and +4.7% year-over-year, affecting pricing of Canadian exports to the UK.36 The FTSE 100 closed at 10,608.90, up 34.11% year-over-year, outperforming the DAX's +18.74% gain over the same period.36 Brent crude — the dominant North Sea benchmark — settled at US$90.38/bbl on April 17, following the Strait of Hormuz reopening, down from a peak above US$118/bbl earlier in the period.15 The 150 basis point rate gap between the BoE and the BoC mirrors the Fed-BoC differential, reinforcing CAD cross-rate pressures.
